sections.html:
Simpson County sits on Kentucky's southern edge against the Tennessee line, in the Pennyroyal Plateau region. Franklin is its only city and its seat of government. The county had 20,788 residents in July 2025, up from 19,595 in 2020, living in 9,172 housing units and 8,025 households. The 2020 census counted 10,176 people in Franklin, so about half the county lives in town and the rest in farm and small community settings.

Warren County borders it on the north, Allen on the east and Logan on the west. Franklin's Planning and Zoning Commission follows its Franklin Forward comprehensive plan, which covers land use, housing and community facilities, and the zoning map is posted on the city site.

Owners hold two thirds of the occupied homes, so most sales involve a house with a long-term resident rather than a landlord.

The Property Valuation Administrator puts every parcel on the roll at fair cash value as of January 1, as Section 172 of the Kentucky Constitution requires. Setting rates and taking payments belong to other offices. The January 1 rule matters at a sale, because a buyer who closes later in the year may never see the bill. If one does not arrive, call the Sheriff at 270-586-7425. The PVA answers at 270-586-4261 on weekdays from 8 to 4.

sections.h2: Who sends and collects the bills
sections.html:
Three offices share the job. The County Clerk prepares and prints the bills and records deeds, the Sheriff collects the county and school portions, and the City of Franklin runs its own tax office at 117 W Cedar for city bills. Franklin's commission sets the city rates using a state formula, and the city office treats a postmark as proof of on-time payment.

City bills follow the deed records in the clerk's office on January 1. When a property sold afterward, the previous owner remains the city taxpayer, and the city office gives original bills only to the addressee. An escrow company that wants an electronic copy of the billing register pays $100, while substitute bills and master payment lists are provided at no charge.

KRS 134.015 sets the schedule. A bill settled in full by November 1 earns 2 percent off. The printed amount carries no penalty through December 31, January adds 5 percent, and 10 percent applies after January ends. City issue, penalty and delinquent dates vary each year, so read the dates printed on each bill.

Anyone with an interest in the property, such as a tenant or a lender, may pay a delinquent bill without the owner's permission if the Sheriff is shown proof, and a payer can ask to be treated as a transferee (KRS 134.119). After the Sheriff files unpaid claims with the County Clerk, the clerk holds them as certificates of delinquency.

An appeal begins with a conference at the PVA's office. KRS 133.045 keeps the real property roll open for inspection for 13 days from early May, six days a week, and the conference must be requested before that period closes. If you still disagree afterward, file with the County Clerk, and three local residents hear the case informally, with no attorney required.

The local assessment board has three year terms and meets once a year, with seats filled by the city, the Fiscal Court and the county judge. Bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal or photos of damage. A losing owner can carry the case to the state's tax appeals board.

sections.h2: City rules that can hold up a sale
sections.html:
Franklin applies the International Property Maintenance Code through its Code Enforcement department, which takes yard sale permits and public nuisance complaints through its citizen portal. The Planning and Zoning Commission follows KRS Chapter 100, and its staff can be reached at 270-596-2756. The city also keeps a lienholder notification process listed among its services.

A home with a nuisance complaint, an unpaid city tax bill or a permit left open is harder to close. Ask city staff about open cases at an address before you list, and confirm county and city tax payoffs separately.

sections.h2: What a seller owes at closing
sections.html:
Kentucky's deed transfer tax falls on the seller: 50 cents on each $500 of price, taken by the County Clerk at the recording counter (KRS 142.050). Add prorated property tax, any lien payoff and agent fees if you list. Owners who qualify for the homestead or disability exemption should confirm with the PVA that it is on file before the sale, since the PVA administers both. A cash offer avoids agent fees and repair demands, which can matter for an older farmhouse or a rental needing work, but the net after payoffs is the number to compare.

  • PVA: assessments, exemptions and the appeals conference, 270-586-4261.
  • Sheriff, 203 E. Kentucky Ave: collects county tax bills, 270-586-7425.
  • County Clerk, 105 E Kentucky St: prepares tax bills and records deeds, 270-586-8161.

sections.h2: Selling a house with taxes still owed
sections.html:
Two bills can be open on a Franklin address, one from the county and one from the city, so ask for a payoff from each. Get the county figure from the Sheriff and the city figure from the tax office at 117 W Cedar. Both can be paid out of the sale proceeds at closing.

If a lender escrows your taxes, check that the payment actually reached the Sheriff and the city. Then gather your homestead or disability exemption paperwork, the latest bills, and any notices about open nuisance or permit cases. A cash buyer will usually accept the house as is, which removes the repair requests that often come after a buyer's inspection.

sections.h2: Paperwork to gather before you sell
sections.html:
Collect the latest county and city tax bills, proof of any homestead or disability exemption, and a payoff letter from your lender. If you own farm ground or a house outside the city limits, you will only have the county bill, which is simpler. Inside Franklin, expect both.

Call the County Clerk to confirm the deed on record matches the name on your sale contract. A mismatch, such as an old deed that never added a spouse, can stall a closing. Franklin's Code Enforcement department can tell you about any open nuisance case, and the Planning and Zoning staff can confirm how the lot is zoned. Taking care of these early lets you accept an offer without conditions hanging over the sale.

faqs.q: Does Franklin bill its own property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Franklin sets rates through its commission and runs a tax office at 117 W Cedar, open weekdays until 4 p.m. Central time. Houses inside city limits get two bills, one from the county and one from the city.

faqs.q: Who is billed if I buy a Simpson County house after January 1?
faqs.a: The former owner is the taxpayer of record for that year. The PVA mails the bill to the new owner when it can, and a buyer who receives nothing can call the Sheriff at 270-586-7425.

faqs.q: When does the Simpson County early payment discount end?
faqs.a: On November 1. Full payment by then takes 2 percent off, and the face amount holds through December 31 under KRS 134.015. Penalties of 5 and then 10 percent follow.

faqs.q: Where is a Simpson County assessment appeal filed?
faqs.a: After a PVA conference, file with the County Clerk at 105 E Kentucky St. The conference has to happen while the roll is open for inspection, which starts in early May.

faqs.q: What deed tax comes out of a Simpson County sale?
faqs.a: Fifty cents per $500 of price, with a partial block counted whole. The County Clerk collects it at recording.
